extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students and instructors (readers of Proofs from THE BOOK)
extracted.subtask_description: Produce clear, rigorous proofs and constructions in elementary set theory (countability, cardinalities, bijections, Cantor–Bernstein) and classical inequalities (Cauchy–Schwarz, AM-GM), and explicit enumerations/constructions (Calkin–Wilf, Stern sequence). Emphasis on presenting constructions, verifying defining properties, and proving uniqueness/optimality conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calkin–Wilf tree node construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every node i/j has two sons: the left son is i/(i+j) and the right son is (i+j)/j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit recursive rule is the basis for enumerating all positive reduced rationals without duplicates; proofs and algorithms should use these left/right son formulas to generate or traverse the listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractions in the tree are reduced
rubrics_metrics.description: All fractions in the tree are reduced, that is, if r/s appears in the tree, then r and s are relatively prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify by induction from the top 1/1: if r and s are relatively prime then r and r+s, and s and r+s, are relatively prime. A clear base case and inductive step are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustiveness of the tree (every reduced fraction appears)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every reduced fraction r/s > 0 appears in the tree (proof by induction on r + s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction on r+s: smallest is 1/1; if r > s consider r−s/s and its right son; if r < s consider r/(s−r) and its left son. A proof must consider both cases and show the construction reaches any given reduced fraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness in the tree (no duplicates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every reduced fraction appears exactly once (use induction and the observation that non-top nodes are either <1 or >1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue by induction and by considering whether a node is a left or right son; show duplicates would force contradictions with earlier sum-based induction. Address boundary cases explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successor denominator–numerator property
rubrics_metrics.description: The denominator of the n-th fraction equals the numerator of the (n+1)-st fraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove for base cases and then treat left-son/right-son and boundary positions; use induction on the level/position in the level-by-level listing and handle right-boundary and interior cases explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence for Stern's diatomic sequence b(n)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive these recursions from the tree structure (node b(n)/b(n+1) has sons b(2n+1)/b(2n+2) and b(2n+2)/b(2n+3)). To identify sequences, verify initial condition and recursion fully determine b(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of b(n) as hyperbinary counts
rubrics_metrics.description: b(n) = h(n) where h(n) counts hyper-binary representations of n (each power of 2 used at most twice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show h(n) satisfies the same recursion (and initial value) as b(n) to conclude equality. Provide examples (e.g., representations of 6) and verify combinatorial counting matches recursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for successor in Calkin–Wilf (Newman)
rubrics_metrics.description: The successor function f(x) = 1 / (⌊x⌋ + 1 − {x}) maps a rational x to the next element in the Calkin–Wilf listing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by representing x as the k-fold right son of the left son of some y and translate k = ⌊x⌋ and {x} = y/(1+y). Give the algebraic derivation and handle fractional/integral parts and boundary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm to find the n-th Calkin–Wilf fraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Express n in binary n = (b_k ... b1 b0)_2 and follow digits from s/t = 0/1, where bi = 1 means 'take right son' (add denominator to numerator) and bi = 0 means 'take left son' (add numerator to denominator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the path interpretation on the Calkin–Wilf tree, give worked example (e.g., n=25=(11001)_2 gives 7/5), and indicate how to invert (fraction -> position) similarly via binary path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonalization for uncountability
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove (0,1] (or R) is uncountable, write a hypothetical listing rn = 0.a_{n1}a_{n2}... and build b with digits bn chosen different from ann (e.g., from {1,2}) so b differs from every rn on diagonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the construction of bn and verify the resulting b belongs to (0,1] but cannot be any listed rn. Address unique decimal expansions (non-terminating) to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit bijections between intervals and the line
rubrics_metrics.description: Give an explicit bijection f:(0,1] -> (0,1) (piecewise maps on dyadic subintervals) and argue ranges cover desired subranges; use central projection to map (0,1) to R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the piecewise formula, check bijectivity by checking images of successive pieces (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ... ranges), and show composition with projection yields bijection to R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor bijection R^2 -> R (interleaving digit-groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Map (x,y) in (0,1]^2 to z in (0,1] by writing non-terminating decimal expansions and alternating groups between next nonzero digits: first x-group, then y-group, etc.; inverses read off groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain grouping by including next nonzero digit to avoid termination ambiguities, show resulting z is non-terminating, and give algorithm to recover x and y from z to prove bijectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor–Bernstein bijection construction via chains
rubrics_metrics.description: If injections f:M->N and g:N->M exist, align M∪N into chains by alternately applying f and g (forward and backward) and classify chains into four cases; define bijection by mapping mi -> ni in each chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the four chain types (finite cycles, two-way infinite, one-way infinite starting in M, one-way infinite starting in N), and give explicit F mapping in each case; prove injectivity/surjectivity of constructed F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal argument for |P(M)| > |M|
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a bijection φ:N⊆M -> P(M) and define U = {m ∈ N : m ∉ φ(m)}. Then φ(u)=U leads to contradiction whether u∈U or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame as the classical Cantor diagonal (or barber paradox) argument; show no bijection from M onto P(M) can exist, hence |P(M)|>|M|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving existence of next larger cardinal
rubrics_metrics.description: To every cardinal m there exists a definite next larger cardinal: consider set K of cardinals > m and ≤ some n, take initial ordinals ω_p and pick smallest to get next cardinal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-ordering of ordinals and initial ordinal representatives; state the proposition and sketch how minimal initial ordinal yields desired next cardinal. Reference ordinal/cardinal basics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of m many countable sets has size ≤ m
rubrics_metrics.description: If {A_α} is a family of size m (infinite cardinal) of countable sets, then the union ⋃_α A_α has size at most m (use well-ordering and replacement of indices by countable blocks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch strategy: assume disjointness, well-order index set by initial ordinal ω_m, replace each α by countable ordered B_α, form >M, find bijection from M to ⋃A_α via constructed bijections on blocks; specify handling of countable unions and reindexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Schwarz proof via positivity of quadratic
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider |x a + b|^2 as a quadratic in x: nonnegativity implies discriminant ⟨a,b⟩^2 − |a|^2|b|^2 ≤ 0, yielding ⟨a,b⟩^2 ≤ |a|^2|b|^2; equality iff a and b are linearly dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the quadratic expression, justify nonnegativity (unless trivial zero vector), compute discriminant and conclude inequality; discuss equality case and handle trivial vector cases separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: AM–GM via Cauchy's nonstandard induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a1...an ≤ ((a1+...+an)/n)^n by base n=2 and two steps: (A) P(n)⇒P(n−1) and (B) P(n) & P(2) ⇒ P(2n), yielding the full inequality; equality iff all ai equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give clear formulation of P(n), execute the two reduction/extension steps algebraically as in the text, and show how repeated application yields all n. Include treatment of harmonic≤geometric by applying to reciprocals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted AM–GM via integral method (Alzer)
rubrics_metrics.description: For positive a_i and weights p_i with Σ p_i = 1, prove (∏ a_i^{p_i}) ≤ Σ p_i a_i by comparing integrals and using density of certain sets; deduce equality characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present Alzer's integral inequality approach: locate G between ordered a_k, set up integrals with nonnegative integrands, rewrite to obtain A/G − 1 ≥ 0 and reduce to logarithmic identity; emphasize choosing parameters so series converges and integrals are defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inequalities in polynomial root location (Laguerre)
rubrics_metrics.description: If polynomial x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + a_0 has all real roots, apply Cauchy inequality to vector of roots and ones to derive bounds: roots lie in interval with endpoints −a_{n-1}/n ± (n−1)/n * sqrt(...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate coefficient comparisons via Vieta relations, form sums of squares, apply Cauchy–Schwarz to (y1,...,y_{n-1}) and (1,...,1) to bound y, and algebraically solve quadratic inequality to produce the interval for roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds for area vs tangential triangle/rectangle for real-root polynomials (Erdős–Gallai)
rubrics_metrics.description: For real-root polynomial f of degree n≥2 with f(±1)=0 and f>0 on (−1,1), show (2/3)T ≤ A ≤ (2/3)R, with equality only for n=2, using AM–GM and related inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain definitions of A (integral of f), T (area of tangential triangle), R (rectangle area 2f(b)), compute tangents and their intersection, and then apply inequality techniques (AM–GM, induction) specialized to polynomials with real roots to get stated bounds; treat n=2 equality case separately.
